description: AI, data centres and infrastructure: the pieces, how they depend on each other, who acts, and what has gone wrong.

records.title: Alibaba Cloud
records.description: Alibaba Cloud is the cloud and AI arm of the Chinese company Alibaba, and makes the Qwen family of models.
records.text: In February 2025 Alibaba said it would invest at least 380 billion yuan (about $53 billion) in cloud and AI infrastructure over three years. Its Qwen models are released in many sizes, and many of them are open-weight. Alibaba Cloud's own Model Studio service is built on Qwen models.

records.title: Amazon Web Services
records.description: Amazon's cloud business, the largest renter of computing power; its parent, Amazon, is a large investor in Anthropic.
records.text: Most websites and apps you use run somewhere on rented servers, and AWS rents more of them than anyone. It also designs its own AI chips (Trainium).

records.title: Amazon–Anthropic partnership
records.description: Amazon has invested $8 billion in Anthropic, and Amazon Web Services is Anthropic's main cloud and training partner.
records.text: Amazon invested $4 billion in Anthropic by March 2024 and another $4 billion in November 2024, bringing its total to $8 billion. As part of the deal, AWS became Anthropic's "primary cloud and training partner," and Anthropic works with Amazon's chip designers on future Trainium chips. AWS also built Project Rainier, a cluster of Trainium2 chips that Anthropic uses to build and run Claude.

records.title: Anthropic
records.description: A lab founded in 2021 by former OpenAI staff, which makes the Claude models and presents itself as safety-focused.
records.text: Anthropic sells access to its Claude models to people and companies. Amazon and Google are both large investors, and both rent it computing power.

records.title: Anthropic–Google TPU deal
records.description: In October 2025 Anthropic agreed to use up to one million Google TPU chips, with well over a gigawatt of capacity online in 2026.
records.text: Anthropic announced the expansion on October 23, 2025 and said it was worth tens of billions of dollars. Google mentioned Anthropic's plan in its November 2025 announcement of Ironwood, its seventh-generation TPU. Anthropic trains and runs Claude on three kinds of chips at once: Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium and Nvidia GPUs, so it is not tied to a single chipmaker.

records.title: Anthropic–Microsoft–Nvidia deal
records.description: In November 2025 Anthropic committed to buy $30 billion of Microsoft Azure computing, while Nvidia and Microsoft agreed to invest in Anthropic.
records.text: The deal was announced on November 18, 2025. Anthropic agreed to buy $30 billion of Azure compute and to contract up to one gigawatt of capacity, running on Nvidia Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Nvidia planned to invest up to $10 billion in Anthropic and Microsoft up to $5 billion. The two companies investing in Anthropic are the same ones selling it computing power and chips.

records.title: Colossus (xAI, Memphis)
records.description: Colossus is xAI's AI training supercomputer in Memphis, Tennessee, which came online in September 2024 with 100,000 Nvidia H100 chips.
records.text: Colossus came online over Labor Day weekend 2024 with 100,000 Nvidia H100 chips, and Elon Musk said it was built "from start to finish" in 122 days. It was built to train xAI's Grok-3 model. Musk said at the time that it would double to 200,000 chips, including 50,000 of Nvidia's newer H200s.

records.title: CoreWeave
records.description: CoreWeave is an AI cloud company that rents computing power to AI labs.
records.text: CoreWeave was founded in 2017 and listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange in March 2025; it says it works with 9 of the 10 leading AI model makers. Its contracts with OpenAI are worth up to about $22.4 billion in total: up to $11.9 billion in March 2025, up to $4 billion more in May 2025, and up to $6.5 billion more in September 2025. In November 2026 Nvidia named CoreWeave as one of the first places where its Vera Rubin NVL72 racks were running.

records.title: DeepSeek
records.description: A Chinese lab whose R1 model (January 2025) matched leading models at a reported fraction of the cost, and released its weights.
records.text: DeepSeek trained under US export controls that limited which Nvidia chips it could buy. Its success raised the question of whether controlling chips can control who builds AI.

records.title: Google DeepMind
records.description: Google's AI lab, formed in 2023 by merging DeepMind (London) with Google Brain; it makes the Gemini models.
records.text: Unlike most labs, Google designs its own AI chips (TPUs), runs its own data centres and owns the products people already use (Search, Gmail, YouTube), so it can put a model in front of billions of people without renting anything.

records.title: Meta
records.description: Facebook's parent company, which releases its Llama models as open weights that anyone can download and run.
records.text: Giving the weights away is a strategy: other people build on Meta's models instead of a rival's. It also means Meta cannot take a model back once it is out.

records.title: Microsoft
records.description: OpenAI's largest investor, which runs OpenAI's models in its Azure cloud and builds them into Windows and Office.
records.text: Microsoft is a hyperscaler: one of a few companies that own enough data centres to rent computing power to everyone else. In 2024 it signed a deal to buy power from a Three Mile Island reactor that is to be restarted (planned for 2027–28).

records.title: Microsoft–OpenAI partnership
records.description: Microsoft is a major investor in OpenAI whose Azure cloud trained ChatGPT and GPT-4; the two rewrote their deal in October 2025.
records.text: ChatGPT, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were trained on supercomputers built with Microsoft's Azure cloud. Under the new agreement of October 28, 2025, Microsoft holds about 27% of OpenAI, valued at about $135 billion, and OpenAI agreed to buy an extra $250 billion of Azure services. Microsoft also gave up its right of first refusal to be OpenAI's compute provider.

records.title: Mistral AI
records.description: Mistral AI is a French AI lab, founded in April 2023, that also releases the weights of some of its models.
records.text: Mistral AI was founded in April 2023 by Arthur Mensch, Guillaume Lample and Timothée Lacroix. In June 2025 it announced Mistral Compute, a platform planned with Nvidia that would deploy 18,000 Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra GPUs in its first phase. In 2025 the chip-equipment maker ASML invested about $1.5 billion in Mistral and became its largest shareholder. In October 2026 Mistral released the weights of a model called Le Chonk.

records.title: OpenAI
records.description: The lab that released ChatGPT in November 2022, the product that made chatbots a mass habit.
records.text: Founded in 2015 as a non-profit research lab, OpenAI added a capped-profit company in 2019 to raise money for computing power. In October 2025 that company became a public benefit corporation, still controlled by the non-profit (now the OpenAI Foundation). Microsoft is its largest investor. It trains the GPT models and sells access to them through ChatGPT and an API.

records.title: OpenAI–AMD deal
records.description: In October 2025 OpenAI agreed to deploy 6 gigawatts of AMD GPUs, starting with 1 gigawatt of MI450 chips in the second half of 2026.
records.text: The deal was announced on October 6, 2025. As part of it, AMD gave OpenAI a warrant to buy up to 160 million AMD shares. OpenAI has also made chip deals with Broadcom and Cerebras, and has said it needs more computing power than Nvidia alone can provide.

records.title: OpenAI–Broadcom custom chip deal
records.description: In October 2025 OpenAI and Broadcom agreed to build 10 gigawatts of AI chips designed by OpenAI.
records.text: OpenAI designs the accelerators and systems, and Broadcom develops and deploys them. The racks are planned to start going in during the second half of 2026 and to be finished by the end of 2029. OpenAI has said it needs more computing power than Nvidia alone can provide.

records.title: OpenAI–Nvidia deal
records.description: In September 2025 OpenAI and Nvidia signed a letter of intent for at least 10 gigawatts of Nvidia systems and up to $100 billion of Nvidia investment, which was later replaced by a $30 billion investment.
records.text: The September 22, 2025 letter of intent planned the first gigawatt for the second half of 2026 on Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform. By February 2026 no contract had been signed and no money had changed hands. In March 2026 Nvidia instead invested $30 billion in OpenAI's $122 billion funding round. An OpenAI infrastructure executive, quoted in February 2026, wrote: "Our entire compute fleet runs on Nvidia GPUs."

records.title: OpenAI's $122 billion funding round
records.description: In March 2026 OpenAI closed a $122 billion funding round that valued it at $852 billion.
records.text: Amazon committed up to $50 billion, with $15 billion up front and $35 billion depending on conditions; Nvidia and SoftBank each put in $30 billion. As part of Amazon's investment, OpenAI committed to use 2 gigawatts of Amazon's Trainium chip capacity. Two of the largest investors, Amazon and Nvidia, also sell OpenAI computing power and chips.

records.title: The Stargate Project
records.description: Stargate is a plan announced in January 2025 to spend $500 billion over four years on AI data centres in the United States for OpenAI.
records.text: OpenAI announced Stargate on January 21, 2025, saying $100 billion would be deployed right away and up to $500 billion over four years. The first equity funders named were SoftBank, OpenAI, Oracle and MGX, and the technology partners were Arm, Microsoft, Nvidia, Oracle and OpenAI. Building started in Texas. The $500 billion was a plan for future spending, not money already spent.

records.title: xAI
records.description: xAI is Elon Musk's AI company, which makes the Grok models and has been owned by SpaceX since February 2026.
records.text: xAI built Colossus, a supercomputer in Memphis, Tennessee, to train its Grok models. On February 2, 2026, SpaceX announced it had acquired xAI, which had already merged with the social network X. Musk gave AI's power needs as the reason, writing that "global electricity demand for AI simply cannot be met with terrestrial solutions" and pointing to data centres in space.

records.title: A breakthrough
records.description: A new model or method changes what is possible, or what it costs, and the market moves.
records.text: After DeepSeek's R1 showed strong results at low reported cost, Nvidia's stock fell about 17% on January 27, 2025, its largest one-day loss in market value at the time.

records.title: A frontier model
records.description: The largest, most capable AI model of its moment: a file of billions of numbers (weights) learned from data.
records.text: "Frontier" just means the leading edge, which moves every few months. Physically, a model is its weights: a very large file that has to sit in the memory of many chips to run.

records.title: An AI agent
records.description: A model given tools (a browser, a terminal, a budget) and a goal, then left to take steps on its own.
records.text: Is an agent a player, an NPC, or a piece of equipment a player uses? That is the question this entry is here to raise. It acts, but on someone's instructions; it can be given a goal and keep going after the person who set it walks away.

records.title: An open-weight model
records.description: A model whose weights are published for anyone to download, run and change, like Meta's Llama or DeepSeek's R1.
records.text: Open weights spread a model beyond its maker's control: good for researchers and small companies, harder to police. Once released, they cannot be recalled.

records.title: ChatGPT
records.description: ChatGPT is OpenAI's chatbot, released on November 30, 2022.
records.text: ChatGPT was first built by fine-tuning a model from OpenAI's GPT-3.5 series, which finished training in early 2022. It and GPT-3.5 were trained on Microsoft Azure's AI supercomputing infrastructure. By October 2026 OpenAI said more than 1.2 billion people used ChatGPT each week.

records.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2
records.description: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are two versions of the same Anthropic model, released on November 9, 2026.
records.text: Fable 5.2 has safeguards for cybersecurity and biology and is open to all users; Mythos 5.2 lacks some of those safeguards and is limited to vetted organisations, such as cybersecurity professionals and life sciences researchers who apply. Fable 5.2 is available on AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure, priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

records.title: Claude Opus 5.5
records.description: Claude Opus 5.5 is an Anthropic model released on September 22, 2026, the first of its Claude 5.5 family.
records.text: Anthropic made Opus 5.5 available on its own platform and on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. It costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, and Anthropic said it runs about 40% cheaper than Opus 5.

records.title: DeepSeek-R1
records.description: DeepSeek-R1 is a reasoning model released by DeepSeek on January 20, 2025, with its weights under the MIT license.
records.text: DeepSeek said R1's performance was comparable to OpenAI's o1 reasoning model. Its code and weights were released under the MIT license, which allows commercial use and allows others to train smaller models from its outputs. Developers can also use it through DeepSeek's API.

records.title: DeepSeek-V3
records.description: DeepSeek-V3 is an open-weight model from the Chinese lab DeepSeek, described in December 2024, with 671 billion parameters.
records.text: DeepSeek-V3 is a "mixture of experts" model: it has 671 billion parameters in total, but uses only 37 billion of them for each token. It was trained on 14.8 trillion tokens, and DeepSeek said full training took 2.788 million GPU hours on Nvidia H800 chips.

records.title: DeepSeek-V4
records.description: DeepSeek-V4 is a pair of open-weight models released in preview by DeepSeek on April 24, 2026.
records.text: DeepSeek-V4-Pro has 1.6 trillion parameters in total, with 49 billion used for each token; DeepSeek-V4-Flash has 284 billion, with 13 billion used for each token. Both can work with up to 1 million tokens of context. The weights were published on Hugging Face.

records.title: Gemini 3
records.description: Gemini 3 is a Google model family whose first model, Gemini 3 Pro, was released in preview on November 18, 2025.
records.text: Google put Gemini 3 Pro into the Gemini app, Google Search's AI Mode for paying subscribers, and its developer and business tools on the same day. A deeper-reasoning version, Gemini 3 Deep Think, was held back for more safety testing.

records.title: Gemini 4 Argon
records.description: Gemini 4 Argon is a Google flagship model announced on September 30, 2026, first given only to a limited group of cyber defenders.
records.text: Google built Argon for long, complex tasks such as coding, legal and finance work, and cybersecurity defence. It went first to trusted cyber defenders through a program called Fairwind. Google said a wider release would follow after more safety testing, starting with paying API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers.

records.title: GPT-3
records.description: GPT-3 is a language model with 175 billion parameters, described by OpenAI in May 2020.
records.text: The GPT-3 paper showed that a much larger language model could do many tasks from only a few examples, without extra training for each task.

records.title: GPT-4
records.description: GPT-4 is a large OpenAI model released on March 14, 2023 that accepts both images and text.
records.text: To train GPT-4, OpenAI rebuilt its deep learning software and, with Microsoft's Azure, designed a supercomputer for the job. OpenAI did not publish how many parameters GPT-4 has. Image input was at first only a research preview.

records.title: GPT-5
records.description: GPT-5 is an OpenAI model released on August 7, 2025 to all ChatGPT users, including free users.
records.text: GPT-5 combines a fast model for most questions, a deeper reasoning model for hard ones, and a router that chooses between them. Free users have lower usage limits and move to a smaller model, GPT-5 mini, when they reach them.

records.title: GPT-6
records.description: GPT-6 is OpenAI's model family introduced in 2026, rolled out to all ChatGPT users from October 7, 2026.
records.text: OpenAI first introduced GPT-6 models for paying customers in September 2026. On October 7, 2026 it began rolling GPT-6 out to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users, and to the Free and Go tiers the next day. OpenAI said the model was built for the more than 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week.

records.title: gpt-oss
records.description: gpt-oss is a pair of open-weight models released by OpenAI on August 5, 2025 under the Apache 2.0 license.
records.text: gpt-oss-120b has about 117 billion parameters and runs on a single 80 GB GPU. gpt-oss-20b has about 21 billion parameters and runs on devices with 16 GB of memory. Because they fit on one chip, people can run them on their own hardware instead of in a lab's data centre.

records.title: Kimi K2
records.description: Kimi K2 is an open-weight model from Moonshot AI with one trillion parameters, published in July 2025.
records.text: Kimi K2 has 1 trillion parameters in total, with 32 billion used for each token. Moonshot AI trained it on 15.5 trillion tokens and released the weights under a modified MIT license.

records.title: Llama 3.1 405B
records.description: Llama 3.1 405B is an open-weight model from Meta, released on July 23, 2024, with about 405 billion parameters.
records.text: Meta trained it on more than 15 trillion tokens of text using more than 16,000 Nvidia H100 GPUs. Anyone could download its weights, and Meta changed its license so developers could use its outputs, including those of the 405B model, to improve other models.

records.title: Model weights
records.description: The numbers a model learns in training. Whoever has the weights has the model.
records.text: Weights are the most valuable thing a lab owns and the easiest to copy: a leak or a theft hands over months of computing in one file. That is why labs guard them, and why open-weight releases are a deliberate choice.

records.title: Qwen3
records.description: Qwen3 is a family of open-weight models released by Alibaba's Qwen team on April 29, 2025.
records.text: The largest Qwen3 model has 235 billion parameters in total, with 22 billion used for each token. The family was trained on about 36 trillion tokens, and it covers 119 languages and dialects. The smaller "dense" models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

records.title: Serving a model (inference)
records.description: Answering users' requests, one at a time, millions of times a day. Each answer costs chips, power and money.
records.text: Training happens once; serving happens forever. As more people use a model, the cost of running it can outgrow the cost of making it.

records.title: Training a model
records.description: Running thousands of chips for weeks or months to turn training data into model weights.
records.text: The most expensive single thing a lab does, and a gamble: you learn how good the model is only at the end.

records.title: Training data
records.description: The text, images, code and recordings a model learns from: much of the public web, books, and paid-for labels.
records.text: Much training text starts from web crawls such as Common Crawl, a free archive of billions of web pages. Then it is filtered, deduplicated and supplemented with human-written examples and ratings.

records.title: A chip shortage
records.description: Demand for chips outruns what fabs can make, and everyone waits.
records.text: From 2020 to 2023, a global shortage of chips stalled car factories and made game consoles hard to buy. AI chips have since been scarce for a different reason: everyone wants the same ones.

records.title: A fab (chip factory)
records.description: A semiconductor fabrication plant: a building costing billions where chips are printed onto silicon wafers in ultra-clean rooms.
records.text: Fabs need extremely pure water, steady power, rare gases and machines from a handful of suppliers. Building one takes years.

records.title: AMD Instinct GPUs (MI300X, MI355X, MI450)
records.description: Instinct is AMD's line of data-centre GPUs for AI.
records.text: By June 2025, Microsoft said the MI300X was running models on Azure, and Meta said it was widely used to run Llama 3 and Llama 4. AMD said its MI350 series would be broadly available in the second half of 2025, with Oracle among the first to adopt the MI355X, and previewed a rack called Helios built on the next MI400 series. OpenAI plans to start deploying 1 gigawatt of MI450 chips in the second half of 2026.

records.title: An EUV lithography machine
records.description: A machine the size of a bus that uses extreme ultraviolet light to print the smallest features on chips. Only ASML makes them.
records.text: Each one is shipped in many crates and costs around $180–200 million (the newest High-NA model about $370 million). Without them, the most advanced chips cannot be made.

records.title: ASML
records.description: A Dutch company, the only maker of the extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines needed for the most advanced chips.
records.text: One company in one small country making a machine nobody else can make is a choke point: whoever controls where its machines can be shipped controls who can make leading chips.

records.title: AWS Trainium
records.description: Trainium is the AI chip that Amazon Web Services designs for training and running models in its own data centres.
records.text: Project Rainier, which Anthropic uses, runs on nearly half a million Trainium2 chips. In December 2025 AWS made Trainium3 generally available: its first 3-nanometre AI chip, with 144 GB of HBM3e memory and up to 144 chips in one server. In 2026 OpenAI also committed to use 2 gigawatts of Trainium capacity.

records.title: Chip foundry market share (April–June 2026)
records.description: In the second quarter of 2026, TSMC earned 72.5% of the revenue of the world's ten largest chip foundries.
records.text: The market research firm TrendForce found that the top ten foundries earned nearly $53.49 billion in the quarter, a record. TSMC took about $40.2 billion, Samsung Foundry $3.26 billion (5.9%), and China's SMIC more than $3 billion (5.4%). A foundry makes chips that other companies design; Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, for example, are made by TSMC.

records.title: Google Ironwood TPU
records.description: Ironwood is Google's seventh-generation TPU, an AI chip Google designs for its own data centres and cloud customers.
records.text: Google announced Ironwood in April 2025. Each chip has 192 GB of HBM memory, and up to 9,216 chips can be linked in one pod, which Google says reaches 42.5 exaflops. In November 2025 Google said Ironwood would be generally available within weeks and that Anthropic planned to use up to one million TPUs. Its previous generation was Trillium, the sixth.

records.title: GPUs (AI chips)
records.description: Graphics processing units: chips that do many simple calculations at once, which is what training a model needs.
records.text: A frontier training run uses tens of thousands of them, wired together and run for months. They are scarce, expensive and controlled by export rules.

records.title: High-bandwidth memory
records.description: Stacked memory chips packed next to an AI chip so the model's weights can be read fast enough. A bottleneck of its own.
records.text: AI chips are often limited by how fast they can read numbers, not how fast they can calculate. A few companies (SK Hynix, Samsung, Micron) make this memory.

records.title: Huawei Ascend chips
records.description: Ascend is the line of AI chips made by the Chinese company Huawei.
records.text: Huawei's Atlas 900 A3 SuperPoD links up to 384 Ascend 910C chips. In September 2025 Huawei published a roadmap: the Ascend 950PR in early 2026, the 950DT at the end of 2026, the 960 at the end of 2027 and the 970 at the end of 2028. It also plans its own high-bandwidth memory, and an Atlas 950 SuperPoD of up to 8,192 chips for the end of 2026. These dates were plans when Huawei announced them.

records.title: Intel Fab 52 (Chandler, Arizona)
records.description: Fab 52 is Intel's newest chip factory, at its Ocotillo campus in Chandler, Arizona, where it makes chips on its 18A process.
records.text: Construction began in late 2021, and by October 2025 mass production on Intel's 18A process was under way. 18A is a 2-nanometre-class process; it is Intel's first to use gate-all-around transistors and to deliver power from the back of the chip. The first 18A products are Intel's Panther Lake laptop processors.

records.title: Intel Ohio One
records.description: Ohio One is Intel's planned chipmaking campus in Licking County, Ohio, whose first fab has been delayed to 2030.
records.text: When Intel broke ground on the nearly 1,000-acre site, it said the first fab could be online by 2025. In February 2025 Intel said it now expects to finish building the first fab in 2030 and the second in 2031.

records.title: Lam Research
records.description: Lam Research is a US maker of chipmaking equipment, mainly machines that deposit and etch thin layers on silicon wafers.
records.text: Lam sells deposition and etch tools, along with strip and clean and measurement equipment. In 2025 it was the third-largest maker of chipmaking equipment, after ASML and Applied Materials, in a market worth $136.2 billion.

records.title: Nvidia
records.description: The company that designs most of the chips (GPUs) AI models are trained on. It designs them; others manufacture them.
records.text: Nvidia began making graphics cards for video games. The same chips turned out to suit the arithmetic of neural networks, and its software (CUDA) made them the default for AI research. It has no factories of its own: TSMC makes its chips.

records.title: Nvidia B200 (Blackwell)
records.description: The B200 is Nvidia's Blackwell-generation GPU, announced in March 2024, made of two chips joined into one.
records.text: Blackwell GPUs have 208 billion transistors and are made by TSMC on a custom process called 4NP. Each one joins two of the largest dies a fab can print, linked at 10 terabytes per second, so they act as a single GPU. Nvidia named AWS, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle, Tesla and xAI among the companies expected to use it.

records.title: Nvidia GB200 NVL72 rack
records.description: The GB200 NVL72 is a liquid-cooled rack from Nvidia that links 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs into one system.
records.text: Nvidia sells it as a whole rack-scale system, not as separate chips, and the 72 GPUs in a rack are linked to work together. Oracle began delivering the first GB200 racks at the Stargate campus in Abilene, Texas in June 2025. Because it is liquid-cooled, the data centre must bring cooling liquid to every rack.

records.title: Nvidia H100
records.description: The H100 is Nvidia's data-centre GPU built on its Hopper architecture.
records.text: The standard H100 has 80 GB of HBM3 memory and draws up to 700 watts. Meta trained Llama 3.1 405B on more than 16,000 of them, and xAI's first Colossus cluster used 100,000.

records.title: Nvidia H200 exports to China
records.description: In January 2026 the US began reviewing licences to export Nvidia H200 chips to China case by case, but by November 2026 Nvidia had stopped shipping them there.
records.text: On January 13, 2026 the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security said it would review licences for the Nvidia H200, the AMD MI325X and similar chips case by case, with conditions such as US third-party testing. Documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee show it had approved more than 879,000 AI chips for Chinese companies by May 2026. In November 2026 Nvidia said: "Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China"; analysts said Beijing had not approved large-scale imports.

records.title: Nvidia Vera Rubin
records.description: Vera Rubin is Nvidia's platform after Blackwell, announced in January 2026 and shipping in volume by November 2026.
records.text: Nvidia announced it at CES on January 5, 2026 as a set of six chips: the Vera CPU, the Rubin GPU, and four networking and data-processing chips. A Vera Rubin NVL72 rack holds 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs. Samsung's HBM4 memory met Nvidia's speed requirement for Rubin. On November 17, 2026 Nvidia said Vera Rubin NVL72 had shipped and was running at CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Nebius.

records.title: Nvidia's data-centre sales, quarter to October 2026
records.description: In the three months to October 25, 2026, Nvidia sold $115.8 billion of products, $107.6 billion of it for data centres.
records.text: Nvidia reported the results on November 17, 2026. Data-centre revenue was up 110% from a year earlier and made up about 93% of all of Nvidia's sales. The figures show how much money is being spent on AI chips.

records.title: Samsung Pyeongtaek campus
records.description: Pyeongtaek is a Samsung chipmaking campus in South Korea with four fabs running and a fifth being built.
records.text: The campus runs four fabs, P1 to P4. In April 2026 P4, a roughly 50 trillion won building, was running at half capacity, with more lines due to start in July and November 2026. Main construction on P5, estimated at more than 80 trillion won, began in April 2026, with operations planned for 2028. Samsung expects its HBM capacity, the memory that sits next to AI chips, to grow about 50% in 2026, and Nvidia is its top customer.

records.title: SK hynix
records.description: SK hynix is a South Korean memory maker and the largest supplier of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI chips.
records.text: According to IDC, SK hynix had 56.4% of HBM revenue in the first quarter of 2026. It began putting wafers into its new M15X fab in Cheongju in early 2026, expects the first cleanroom of its Yongin fab to open in early 2027, and plans an advanced packaging plant in Indiana from the second half of 2028.

records.title: Tokyo Electron
records.description: Tokyo Electron (TEL) is a maker of chipmaking equipment, founded more than 60 years ago.
records.text: TEL sells six kinds of equipment for 300 mm wafers: deposition, lithography coaters and developers, etch, cleaning, wafer probers for testing, and bonding for stacked chips. In 2025 it was the fourth-largest maker of chipmaking equipment.

records.title: TPUs
records.description: Tensor Processing Units: Google's own AI chips, mostly used in its own data centres and rented through Google Cloud, rather than sold as chips.
records.text: Designing your own chips is a way out of depending on Nvidia; Amazon and Microsoft are doing the same.

records.title: TSMC
records.description: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company: the contract manufacturer that makes the most advanced chips for Nvidia, Apple and others.
records.text: TSMC manufactures chips other companies design. Most of the world's most advanced chips are made in its fabs in Taiwan, which is why an earthquake, a drought or a blockade there is a risk for the whole AI industry. Its first Arizona fab is in production, and more are being built there.

records.title: TSMC Arizona (Phoenix)
records.description: TSMC Arizona is TSMC's chipmaking site in Phoenix, its first advanced US site, with one fab in production and more being built.
records.text: TSMC chose Phoenix in 2020, and its planned investment has grown from $12 billion to $265 billion for six chip fabs, two advanced packaging plants and a research centre. Fab 1 has made chips in high volume on TSMC's 4-nanometre process since late 2024. Fab 2 is planned to make 3-nanometre chips from the second half of 2027, and Fab 3, begun in April 2025, is planned for 2-nanometre and smaller processes.

records.title: TSMC Fab 18 (Tainan)
records.description: Fab 18 is TSMC's giant chip factory in the Southern Taiwan Science Park in Tainan, where it makes its 5-nanometre and 3-nanometre chips.
records.text: TSMC calls Fab 18 a GIGAFAB facility. Each of its first eight phases has 58,000 square metres of cleanroom, about twice a standard logic fab, and TSMC's total investment in it will exceed NT$1.86 trillion. Its 3-nanometre process entered volume production there in December 2022.

records.title: A hyperscale data centre
records.description: A warehouse of servers on the scale of a factory, built by a cloud company, drawing as much power as a small city.
records.text: Inside: rows of racks, cooling systems, backup generators and fibre connections. Outside: substations, water lines, fences. AI training has made new ones larger and more power-hungry.

records.title: Anthropic's own data centres (with Fluidstack)
records.description: A $50 billion plan by Anthropic to build its own AI data centres in the United States, starting in Texas and New York.
records.text: Anthropic announced the plan on November 12, 2025, with the company Fluidstack building the sites. The first sites are in Texas and New York, with more planned, and they were scheduled to come online through 2026. Anthropic expected about 2,400 construction jobs and 800 permanent jobs.

records.title: Building a data centre
records.description: Buying land, winning permits, securing power and water, then construction: years before the first server runs.
records.text: Power is often the slowest part: a site is chosen as much for its grid connection as for anything else.

records.title: Closed-loop liquid cooling ('zero-water' design)
records.description: A cooling design where liquid circulates between the chips and outdoor chillers in a sealed loop, so no water evaporates.
records.text: Microsoft began using this design in August 2024. The loop is filled once during construction and then reused, which Microsoft says avoids more than 125 million litres of water a year per datacentre. The trade-off is slightly higher electricity use than evaporative cooling. Microsoft's Fairwater sites in Wisconsin and Atlanta use closed-loop liquid cooling.

records.title: Colossus 1 (Memphis)
records.description: An AI supercomputer built by xAI in a former Electrolux factory in South Memphis, Tennessee.
records.text: xAI started building Colossus 1 in 2024 and filled it with about 100,000 Nvidia H100 GPUs in 122 days, mainly to train its Grok chatbot. Epoch AI, which tracks data centres from satellite images, puts its IT power at about 340 MW and says it is cooled by evaporative cooling towers. In July 2025 the Shelby County Health Department permitted 15 gas turbines at the site (up to 247 MW), after environmental groups said dozens had run without permits. In May 2026 Anthropic agreed to rent all of its computing capacity, more than 300 MW.

records.title: Colossus 2 (Memphis)
records.description: xAI's second and much larger AI data centre, in the Whitehaven area of Memphis, Tennessee.
records.text: Land clearing began in February 2025 and the first computing cluster, about 210 MW, came online in October 2025. Epoch AI estimated the site at about 946 MW of IT power in June 2026, with about 1.5 GW projected for early 2027. Much of its electricity comes from gas turbines just across the state line in Southaven, Mississippi, and it is cooled by air-cooled chillers instead of water towers. xAI is now part of SpaceX, and the site's users include Anthropic and Cursor.

records.title: Cooling
records.description: Fans, chillers, cooling towers and liquid loops that carry the heat away from chips. Some of them evaporate water.
records.text: Almost all the electricity a data centre uses ends up as heat. Getting rid of it is a large share of the cost and, where evaporative cooling is used, of local water use.

records.title: Crusoe's Microsoft campus in Abilene
records.description: A 900 MW AI data centre campus for Microsoft that Crusoe is building next to the Stargate site in Abilene, Texas.
records.text: Crusoe announced the campus in March 2026: two buildings of 336 MW of computing load each, bringing the whole Abilene site to about 2.1 GW. It will run on its own 900 MW power plant on site, separate from the grid ('behind the meter'), with a large battery. Land clearing has begun and the first building is expected to be switched on in mid-2027.

records.title: Data Center Alley (Northern Virginia)
records.description: Loudoun County, Virginia: one of the largest concentrations of data centres in the world.
records.text: Early internet exchange points, cheap land and power drew data centres here, and each new one made the next more likely. A place where an installed base keeps growing.

records.title: Data centre water use
records.description: Data centres use water directly to cool their machines and indirectly through the power plants that make their electricity.
records.text: Berkeley Lab estimated US data centres consumed about 17.5 billion gallons of water directly in 2023, and about 211 billion gallons indirectly through the electricity they used. A large data centre can use up to 5 million gallons a day, about as much as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. Northern Virginia's data centres used close to 2 billion gallons in 2023. Evaporative cooling can strain local water supplies during summer peaks.

records.title: Global data centre electricity use (IEA)
records.description: The International Energy Agency's estimates of how much electricity the world's data centres use, now and by 2030.
records.text: The IEA estimates data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, about 1.5% of the world's electricity, and about 485 TWh in 2025. It expects use to roughly double to about 950 TWh by 2030, around 3% of global electricity. Servers built for AI are the fastest-growing part: the IEA says AI-focused data centres used 50% more electricity in 2025 than in 2024. In the US, data centre use per person was about 540 kWh in 2024 and is projected to pass 1,200 kWh by 2030.

records.title: Google AI hub, Visakhapatnam (India)
records.description: A gigawatt-scale Google AI data centre complex under construction in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, India.
records.text: Google announced the hub in October 2025 and broke ground at Tarluvada on April 28, 2026. It plans to spend $15 billion from 2026 to 2030 on three data centre campuses of nearly 1 GW, built with AdaniConneX and Airtel's Nxtra, plus expanded fibre-optic links. Google says it will pair the hub with new clean power on India's grid.

records.title: Google Council Bluffs (Iowa)
records.description: A Google data centre campus in Council Bluffs, Iowa, filled with AI chips that Google owns.
records.text: Epoch AI's satellite tracking shows new buildings coming online in late 2024, mid-2025 and by mid-2026, for about 237 MW of IT power. The AI chips there are owned by Google, and the campus uses evaporative cooling towers, which cool by letting water evaporate. Google runs many other data centre campuses in the Midwest, including in Omaha, Lincoln, Papillion and Cedar Rapids.

records.title: Google's three new Texas data centres
records.description: Three Google data centres announced in November 2025 for Armstrong County and Haskell County, Texas, as part of a $40 billion investment.
records.text: Google announced the plan on November 14, 2025, calling it its largest investment in any state, to run through 2027. One data centre is in Armstrong County in the Panhandle and two are in Haskell County in West Texas. One Haskell County site will be paired with a new solar and battery plant so it puts less strain on the grid.

records.title: How data centres are cooled
records.description: The main ways data centres remove heat: evaporating water, blowing air, or pumping liquid to the chips.
records.text: The most common method is evaporative cooling, where cooling towers let water evaporate to carry heat away; about 80% of the water a data centre withdraws evaporates. Air-cooled chillers and closed liquid loops use little or no water but need more electricity. Liquid cooling pumps fluid straight to the chips (direct-to-chip) or sinks servers in fluid (immersion), and can cut water use sharply. The IEA says cooling takes about 7% of the electricity in efficient large data centres and over 30% in less efficient ones.

records.title: Ireland's data centres and electricity
records.description: In 2025 data centres used 23% of all metered electricity in Ireland, more than all urban homes combined.
records.text: Ireland's Central Statistics Office counts data centres from electricity meter data. Their share rose from 5% in 2015 to 23% in 2025, when they used 7,663 GWh, up 10% in a year. Urban homes used 18% and rural homes 9%.

records.title: Meta Hyperion (Richland Parish, Louisiana)
records.description: Meta's largest AI data centre campus, under construction in rural Richland Parish, Louisiana.
records.text: Ground was broken in December 2024. In July 2026 Meta said the campus would grow to 5 GW of computing capacity and more than $50 billion of investment, with about 7,500 construction workers at the peak and about 1,000 permanent jobs. Its power comes through the utility Entergy Louisiana, which is building new gas plants for it, and Meta has also paid for roads, water and wastewater upgrades. It was not yet operating when Meta last reported on it.

records.title: Meta Prometheus (New Albany, Ohio)
records.description: Meta's first multi-gigawatt AI training cluster, in the New Albany Business Park near Columbus, Ohio.
records.text: Mark Zuckerberg announced Prometheus in July 2025 and said it would come online in 2026. To build fast, Meta mixed weatherproof tents, rented space and ordinary data centre buildings; the first buildings were running by autumn 2025. Epoch AI estimated about 471 MW of IT power by late summer 2026, rising to about 1 GW by 2028. It is partly powered by Meta's own gas plants on site, and in January 2026 Meta signed nuclear deals to supply it.

records.title: Microsoft Fairwater (Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin)
records.description: Microsoft's first Fairwater AI datacentre, built on land in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, that was first assembled for a Foxconn factory.
records.text: The campus covers 315 acres with three buildings and 1.2 million square feet under roof, and links hundreds of thousands of Nvidia GPUs into one supercomputer. About 90% of it is cooled by a closed loop of liquid that is filled once and reused, with 172 large fans cooling the water outside. Microsoft said it was complete and fully operating on June 23, 2026. A second datacentre next door is under construction and due in 2028, part of more than $7 billion Microsoft is spending in Wisconsin.

records.title: Microsoft Fairwater Atlanta
records.description: Microsoft's second Fairwater AI datacentre, on a QTS campus in Fayetteville, Georgia, south of Atlanta.
records.text: It began operating in October 2025 with the same design as the Wisconsin site: two-storey buildings packed with Nvidia GB200 racks and closed-loop liquid cooling, whose first fill of water equals what about 20 homes use in a year. Microsoft links it to Wisconsin by a dedicated fibre network so that the sites can train one model together; it calls the linked sites an 'AI superfactory'. Epoch AI estimated about 636 MW of IT power by mid-2026, with OpenAI and Microsoft's own AI team among the users.

records.title: Nscale Narvik campus (Norway)
records.description: A 230 MW AI data centre planned near Narvik in northern Norway, first announced as 'Stargate Norway'.
records.text: OpenAI, Nscale and Aker announced it in July 2025, to run on renewable power, mostly hydropower, with closed-loop liquid cooling and waste heat sent to local businesses. In March 2026 the project was folded fully into Nscale. In April 2026 Nscale said Microsoft would rent more than 30,000 Nvidia GPUs there from 2027, and OpenAI said it would get computing there through Microsoft.

records.title: Project Rainier (AWS, Indiana)
records.description: An Amazon Web Services AI cluster built for Anthropic, with a main campus in St. Joseph County, Indiana.
records.text: AWS said in October 2025 that Project Rainier was fully running, less than a year after it was announced, with nearly half a million of Amazon's own Trainium2 chips. Anthropic uses it to train and run Claude and was expected to be on more than a million Trainium2 chips by the end of 2025. The Indiana buildings are cooled with outside air and use no cooling water from October to March.

records.title: Stargate Abilene
records.description: The first and flagship campus of OpenAI's Stargate project, built by Crusoe in Abilene, Texas, and run on Oracle's cloud.
records.text: Construction started in June 2024 and the first two buildings went live in September 2025. The finished campus is planned at eight buildings and 1.2 GW. In September 2026 Oracle said six of the eight buildings, 618 MW and 75% of the campus, had been handed over to the customer. The site draws on two grid substations and also has its own gas turbines and power plant.

records.title: Stargate Saline Township (Michigan)
records.description: A planned 1.4 GW Stargate campus for OpenAI being built by Related Digital in Saline Township, Michigan.
records.text: Construction began at the end of 2025. In April 2026 Epoch AI saw foundation work on the first building and no computing capacity yet, with completion estimated for late 2028. It is one of the Stargate sites outside Texas.

records.title: Stargate Shackelford County (Texas)
records.description: A planned 2 GW Stargate campus for OpenAI being built by Vantage Data Centers in Shackelford County, Texas.
records.text: Construction began in the second half of 2025. In April 2026 Epoch AI saw roofing underway on the first building but no computing capacity running yet, with completion estimated for late 2028. It is one of several Stargate sites in the US meant to follow Abilene.

records.title: Stargate UAE (Abu Dhabi)
records.description: A planned 1 GW AI computing cluster in Abu Dhabi, the first Stargate site outside the United States.
records.text: OpenAI announced Stargate UAE on May 22, 2025 with G42, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco and SoftBank. It is the first phase of a 5 GW data centre campus in the UAE. The first 200 MW was planned to go live in 2026.

records.title: US data centre electricity use (Berkeley Lab)
records.description: A US Department of Energy study found data centres used about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and could use 6.7% to 12% by 2028.
records.text: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found US data centres used about 176 TWh in 2023, up from 58 TWh in 2014. It projected 325 to 580 TWh by 2028, a wide range because no one knows how fast AI will grow. The Department of Energy named AI, data centre construction, new factories and electrification as the drivers.

records.title: Cascade Advanced Energy Facility (Amazon and X-energy)
records.description: A planned plant of small modular nuclear reactors near Richland, Washington, funded by Amazon.
records.text: Energy Northwest plans to build it with X-energy's Xe-100 reactors and Amazon's money, next to the existing Columbia Generating Station. The first phase is four reactors and 320 MW, with an option to grow to 12 reactors and 960 MW. Construction is expected to start by the end of the 2020s, with power in the 2030s. Amazon says its X-energy investment aims to add more than 5 GW of new nuclear power by 2039.

records.title: Clinton nuclear plant and Meta
records.description: A 1,121 MW nuclear plant in Clinton, Illinois, whose output Meta agreed in 2025 to buy for 20 years.
records.text: Clinton had been kept open by a state subsidy that runs out in mid-2027. In June 2025 Constellation and Meta signed a 20-year deal for the plant's output starting in June 2027, which replaces the subsidy and keeps the plant running. The deal also adds 30 MW through upgrades. It keeps an existing plant open rather than building a new one.

records.title: Crane Clean Energy Center (Three Mile Island Unit 1) restart
records.description: A shut-down nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania that Constellation is restarting to sell power to Microsoft.
records.text: Unit 1 at Three Mile Island closed in 2019 for economic reasons; it is separate from Unit 2, which was damaged in the 1979 accident. In September 2024 Constellation signed a 20-year deal to sell its roughly 835 MW to Microsoft and renamed it the Crane Clean Energy Center. In 2026 the Nuclear Regulatory Commission finished its environmental review, but other licence decisions were still pending. Constellation says the restart is ahead of schedule for 2027.

records.title: Dominion Energy's data centre demand (Virginia)
records.description: The amount of power data centres have asked the utility Dominion Energy Virginia to supply.
records.text: At the end of September 2026 Dominion Energy Virginia had about 54.9 GW of data centre capacity in various stages of contracting, up 13% since December 2025. Of that, 12.2 GW was under signed electric service agreements, the firmest stage, where customers must pay even if they use less. The rest is at earlier engineering and construction stages that may not all be built.

records.title: Duane Arnold nuclear plant restart (Iowa)
records.description: Iowa's only nuclear plant, shut in 2020, which NextEra plans to restart to sell power to Google.
records.text: In October 2025 NextEra Energy and Google announced a 25-year deal for Google to buy the 615 MW plant's output for its cloud and AI work in Iowa. NextEra is buying out the two power co-operatives that own 30% of the plant, and one of them will buy the rest of the power. The target is to be back online by early 2029, if regulators approve.

records.title: Entergy Louisiana's gas plants for Meta
records.description: New gas-fired power plants the utility Entergy Louisiana is building to supply Meta's Hyperion data centre.
records.text: On August 20, 2025 Louisiana's Public Service Commission approved three new combined-cycle gas plants: two in Richland Parish next to the data centre, due in late 2028, and one at Entergy's Waterford site, due by the end of 2029. The commission also let Entergy buy up to 1,500 MW of solar power. Entergy says Meta pays its share so other customers are protected from the costs. In July 2026 Meta described a further agreement that funds seven new gas plants, three grid-scale batteries and nuclear upgrades.

records.title: ERCOT large-load queue (Texas)
records.description: The list of big electricity users, mostly data centres, waiting to connect to the Texas grid run by ERCOT.
records.text: By the end of March 2026 the queue held about 410 GW of requests, up nearly 150 GW in two weeks, and about 87% of it was data centres. That is almost five times the Texas grid's record peak demand of 85 GW in 2023. ERCOT projected peak demand could reach 145 GW by 2030.

records.title: Fervo Cape Station geothermal plant (Utah)
records.description: An enhanced geothermal power plant in Beaver County, Utah, that began commercial operation in September 2026.
records.text: Enhanced geothermal power makes electricity from underground heat and can run around the clock. Fervo's first 33 MW unit at Cape Station began commercial operation on September 30, 2026, with about 100 MW planned in the first phase. In September 2026 Google signed a deal for 396 MW from a later phase, due in 2028, as a base for a possible Google data centre in Utah.

records.title: Gas power plants
records.description: The quickest large source of new, round-the-clock power, and a source of carbon emissions.
records.text: Because data centres run all day and night, many new ones are being paired with gas plants, which conflicts with companies' climate pledges.

records.title: Gas turbine backlog
records.description: The waiting list for new gas turbines, which has grown long as data centres and utilities order more power plants.
records.text: In April 2026 GE Vernova, one of the largest turbine makers, had 100 GW of gas turbines under contract or reserved, and only about 10 GW of open slots left for 2029 and 2030 combined. New orders for large turbines took about three years to deliver. About a fifth of the turbines under contract were tied directly to data centres. GE Vernova's leaders said the turbine itself is often not what holds a power project up.

records.title: Google's geothermal tariff in Nevada
records.description: A Nevada arrangement approved in May 2025 that adds 115 MW of Fervo geothermal power to the grid for Google's data centres.
records.text: Google and the utility NV Energy proposed the 'Clean Transition Tariff' in June 2024. NV Energy buys power from a Fervo Energy geothermal project and sells it to Google, and Google pays the extra cost compared with the cheaper solar or gas the utility would otherwise build. Nevada's Public Utilities Commission approved it in May 2025. It supports Google's data centres in Storey County, Nevada.

records.title: Kairos Hermes 2 reactor (Google and TVA)
records.description: A 50 MW advanced nuclear reactor planned in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, whose power Google is buying through the Tennessee Valley Authority.
records.text: In October 2024 Google agreed with Kairos Power to bring up to 500 MW of small modular reactors online. Hermes 2 is the first: in August 2025 Google, Kairos and the Tennessee Valley Authority agreed it would put 50 MW onto TVA's grid, supporting Google data centres in Tennessee and Alabama. It is scheduled to start operating in 2030.

records.title: Meta's nuclear deals for Prometheus (Vistra, TerraPower, Oklo)
records.description: Three nuclear power agreements Meta signed on January 9, 2026 to power its Prometheus AI cluster in Ohio.
records.text: Meta will help pay to extend and expand Vistra's existing nuclear plants in Ohio and Pennsylvania, fund two TerraPower reactors that could produce power by 2032, and back Oklo's planned nuclear campus in Pike County, Ohio, which could start as soon as 2030. Together the projects could add 6.6 GW by 2035. The TerraPower and Oklo reactors have not been built yet.

records.title: Microsoft–Brookfield renewable power deal
records.description: A May 2024 agreement for Brookfield to develop more than 10.5 GW of new renewable power for Microsoft.
records.text: The framework covers wind, solar and other carbon-free power in the US and Europe, to be delivered from 2026 to 2030. It was almost eight times larger than the biggest single corporate power deal signed before it. Individual contracts are signed project by project under the framework.

records.title: Nuclear power
records.description: Steady, low-carbon power that tech companies have started buying directly, including from a reactor being restarted for the purpose.
records.text: In 2024 Microsoft agreed to buy power from a reactor at Three Mile Island that had closed in 2019, and Google and Amazon signed deals for small modular reactors that have not been built yet.

records.title: On-site gas power for data centres
records.description: Gas turbines and engines built at or next to data centres so they can run without waiting for a grid connection.
records.text: The IEA estimates 15 to 27 GW of on-site gas power may serve data centres by 2030, mostly in the US. To be reliable, such plants need 30% to 70% more generating capacity than the load they serve. Gas turbine orders rose about 70% in 2025. Examples include xAI's plant in Southaven, Mississippi, the turbines at the Stargate campus in Abilene, Texas, and Meta's Socrates plants in Ohio.

records.title: PJM capacity auction
records.description: The yearly auction in which PJM, the grid operator for 13 states and Washington, DC, pays power plants to be available in future years.
records.text: PJM serves about 67 million people. In its auction for 2027–28 the price hit the cap of $333.44 per MW per day. In July 2026 the auction for 2028–29 again cleared at the cap, $325, and still fell 6,831 MW short of what PJM needs for reliability. PJM says large new loads such as data centres are increasingly being added to the demand forecast that sets how much power it must buy.

records.title: Socrates gas plants (Meta, Ohio)
records.description: Gas-fired power plants built on site to help power Meta's Prometheus AI cluster in New Albany, Ohio.
records.text: Socrates South had 10 gas turbines in place by March 2026, with about 139 MW of its 200 MW running by late August 2026, according to Epoch AI. Socrates North had its turbines installed by early September 2026 and was projected to run fully by late 2026. A third plant of up to 250 MW is projected for 2028.

records.title: Solar, wind and batteries
records.description: Cheap, clean power that comes and goes with the weather, unless it is paired with storage.
records.text: Companies buy renewable power to meet climate pledges, but matching it to a data centre that never sleeps is hard.

records.title: Talen–Amazon Susquehanna nuclear deal
records.description: A June 2025 deal for Talen Energy to supply up to 1,920 MW from the Susquehanna nuclear plant in Pennsylvania to Amazon's data centres.
records.text: Amazon had bought a data centre campus next to the Susquehanna plant and wanted more power straight from it, but federal regulators (FERC) rejected a plan to raise the amount sent directly. In the new deal the plant's power goes onto the regional grid run by PJM, and Talen sells it to Amazon through the grid. The contract runs to 2042 and reaches full volume by 2032. The companies also plan to look at small modular reactors and at upgrades to squeeze more power from the plant.

records.title: The electricity grid
records.description: The power plants, transmission lines and substations that deliver electricity, and the queue to connect to them.
records.text: AI data centres are adding demand faster than grids planned for. Building new lines can take a decade, which is why some companies now build or buy power plants directly.

records.title: Utilities and grid operators
records.description: The companies and agencies that decide who can connect to the electricity grid, and when.
records.text: A new data centre can wait years for a grid connection. Utilities have to balance its demand against homes and other businesses, and usually pass the cost of new power plants and lines on to customers.

records.title: xAI's Southaven gas turbine plant (Mississippi)
records.description: A gas turbine power plant in Southaven, Mississippi, just across the state line from Memphis, that powers xAI's Colossus 2.
records.text: The plant is run by MZX Tech, an xAI company now part of SpaceX. On March 10, 2026 Mississippi's environmental permit board approved 41 permanent gas turbines to replace 27 that had been running without a permit, which state regulators treated as temporary. Neighbours complain of constant noise and worry about air pollution, and the NAACP sued under the Clean Air Act. In November 2026 the board voted 6-1 to keep the permit, and a federal judge had already let the NAACP lawsuit go ahead.

records.title: 2Africa cable
records.description: A Meta-led undersea internet cable about 45,000 km long that circles Africa and links it to Europe and Asia.
records.text: 2Africa reaches 33 countries and is longer than Earth's circumference; Meta announced on November 17, 2025 that its core system was complete after nearly six years of work. It was built by a consortium of Meta with Bayobab (MTN Group), center3 (stc), CMI, Orange, Telecom Egypt, Vodafone Group and WIOCC. Cables like this carry the traffic between users and the data centres that serve AI models.

records.title: Copper
records.description: The metal in the cables, transformers, switchgear and cooling plates that power and cool data centres.
records.text: An estimated 30 to 40 percent of data-centre construction is electrical work, and all of it uses copper, from the transformers and switchgear that bring power in to the copper plates that cool chips. The bank Macquarie estimated 330,000 to 420,000 tonnes of copper will be used in data centres by 2030. In the United States, two-to-five-year waits for transformers have been a bigger bottleneck than copper itself, and new mines take at least ten years to open.

records.title: Critical minerals
records.description: Gallium, germanium, rare earths, copper, cobalt: the raw materials in chips, magnets, wires and batteries.
records.text: Their mining and refining are concentrated in a few countries, especially China, which restricted exports of gallium and germanium in 2023.

records.title: Dunant cable
records.description: Google's undersea cable across the Atlantic between Virginia Beach and Saint-Hilaire-de-Riez, France.
records.text: Google announced on February 3, 2021 that Dunant was ready for service. It carries 250 terabits per second over 12 fibre pairs, and was the first long-haul undersea cable built with that design. Google owns cables like this so that traffic between its data centres on two continents does not depend on anyone else's network.

records.title: Escondida copper mine
records.description: An open-pit copper mine in Chile's Atacama Desert, described as the world's largest.
records.text: Escondida sits about 3,100 metres up in the Antofagasta Region of Chile and produced about 1.28 million tonnes of copper in its 2024 financial year. BHP owns 57.5 percent and Rio Tinto 30 percent. Mining needs water in one of the driest places on Earth: the mine once pumped groundwater, was ordered by a court in 2024 to pay more than US$8 million in compensation over groundwater extraction, and now runs on a coastal desalination plant.

records.title: Gallium
records.description: A soft metal used to make compound semiconductor chips, LEDs and power electronics.
records.text: Gallium is not mined on its own: it is recovered as a by-product, mostly from bauxite (aluminium ore) and some zinc ores. It goes into gallium arsenide and gallium nitride chips used in electronics, LEDs, power electronics and satellites. In 2024 China produced 98 percent of the world's low-purity gallium, so Chinese export rules can squeeze supply for chipmakers everywhere.

records.title: Germanium
records.description: A semiconductor element used in fibre-optic cables, infrared optics and electronics.
records.text: Germanium is mainly recovered as a by-product of zinc processing, and also from coal fly ash. In 2023 its biggest uses were fibre optics (26 percent) and infrared optics (22 percent), with electronics and solar cells next. China is the world's largest source, which is why its export rules on germanium matter to the companies that build data networks.

records.title: Google's data centre in Canelones, Uruguay
records.description: A Google data centre redesigned to use air cooling after protests during Uruguay's 2023 drought.
records.text: Google's original design would have used up to 7.6 million litres of drinking water a day, during a drought that reached crisis levels in July 2023 and led to protests. Uruguay approved it in August 2024, and Google then committed US$850 million to the site.

records.title: Google's water use in The Dalles
records.description: A 13-month fight in Oregon over whether the public could know how much water Google's data centres use.
records.text: The city of The Dalles, Oregon, sued its local newspaper, The Oregonian, to keep Google's data-centre water use secret as a trade secret. It dropped the case in December 2022 after Google agreed to release the numbers and to publish site-level water data for all its US data centres. Google said its data centres in the city of about 15,000 people used about 274.5 million gallons (about 1 billion litres) of water in a year.

records.title: Heavy rare earth elements
records.description: A group of metals such as dysprosium and terbium used to make strong magnets.
records.text: Rare earth elements are used in magnets for electric vehicles, wind turbines, wireless technology and military equipment. Until 2023 China did 99 percent of the world's processing of heavy rare earths. Since April 2025, exporters of seven of them (samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium) have needed a Chinese licence for every shipment.

records.title: Helium
records.description: A gas chip factories blow over wafers to cool them during etching, with no ready substitute.
records.text: Chipmakers use helium to draw heat away from silicon wafers during etching, and under current processes there is no viable replacement. The United States is the largest producer, followed by Qatar, Algeria and Russia; Qatar makes about 30 percent of the world's supply as a by-product of natural gas. South Korea imports about 65 percent of its helium from Qatar, which makes its big memory-chip makers sensitive to any disruption there.

records.title: MAREA cable
records.description: A 6,644 km undersea cable between Virginia Beach in the United States and Bilbao in Spain.
records.text: MAREA was built by Microsoft, Facebook (now Meta) and the telecom company Telxius and has been in service since April 2018, with a design capacity of 160 terabits per second. It lands at Telxius's Virginia Beach cable landing station, which also hosts the BRUSA cable and Google's Dunant cable. These cables connect the huge cluster of data centres in northern Virginia to Europe.

records.title: Ras Laffan helium shutdown
records.description: In March 2026 drone attacks during the Iran war halted gas and helium production at Qatar's Ras Laffan complex.
records.text: QatarGas halted gas production at Ras Laffan, the world's largest liquefied natural gas plant and the source of Qatar's helium, on March 2, 2026 after Iranian drone attacks, and declared force majeure two days later. Further strikes caused what the company called extensive damage that would take years to repair. Spot helium prices doubled, and about 200 specialised helium containers were stuck in the Middle East. TSMC said it did not expect a significant impact.

records.title: Red Sea cable cuts
records.description: On September 6, 2025 undersea cables in the Red Sea near Jeddah were cut, slowing internet and cloud traffic.
records.text: The internet monitor NetBlocks linked the outages to the SMW4 and IMEWE cable systems near Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and reported degraded connections in Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, the United Arab Emirates and India. Microsoft said traffic on its Azure cloud passing through the Middle East might see increased delays as it was rerouted. Microsoft did not say what caused the cuts; cables can be damaged by ship anchors or deliberate attacks.

records.title: Spruce Pine high-purity quartz
records.description: Ultra-pure quartz from mines around Spruce Pine, North Carolina, used to make the crucibles that melt silicon for chips.
records.text: Two companies, Sibelco and The Quartz Corp, make high-purity quartz from the Spruce Pine mines. An estimated 70 to 90 percent of the crucibles used worldwide to melt polysilicon are made from it, and it also goes into solar panels and fibre-optic cables. Both companies shut down ahead of Hurricane Helene in 2024; Sibelco restarted in October 2024, showing how one small town can be a weak point for the whole chip supply chain.

records.title: Taiwan's 2021 drought
records.description: One of Taiwan's worst droughts, when water was rationed for homes and trucked in for chip factories.
records.text: In 2021, after a year when no typhoon hit the island, some of Taiwan's reservoirs fell to 10 to 15 percent of capacity. Household water was rationed while thousands of trucks carried water to the semiconductor industry, angering farmers whose water had been set aside for them. Chipmaking uses about 20 percent of Taiwan's water. Heavy rain later refilled the reservoirs.

records.title: Ukrainian neon
records.description: Neon gas purified in Ukraine and used in the lasers that print patterns onto chips.
records.text: Neon is used in the lasers for lithography, the step that carves circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. Before 2022 more than half of the world's neon came from a handful of Ukrainian companies, including Ingas in Mariupol and Cryoin in Odesa. Both stopped operating amid Russian attacks in early 2022. Chipmakers had stockpiles and other suppliers, and only about two-fifths of the neon used in chipmaking came from Russia and Ukraine.

records.title: Undersea cables
records.description: Fibre-optic cables on the ocean floor that carry almost all traffic between continents.
records.text: There are a few hundred of them. They can be cut by ship anchors or on purpose, and repair ships are few.

records.title: US 50 percent copper tariff
records.description: A US tariff of 50 percent on imported semi-finished copper products, including cables and electrical components, from August 1, 2025.
records.text: On July 30, 2025 President Trump signed a proclamation putting a 50 percent tariff on imported semi-finished copper products such as wire, rods, pipes and tubes, and on copper-heavy parts such as cables, connectors and electrical components. It took effect on August 1, 2025. Raw inputs such as copper ore, concentrates and cathodes were left out. The parts it covers are the same kinds of parts that go into data centres and power lines.

records.title: Water
records.description: Ultra-pure water to wash chips in fabs, and water evaporated to cool some data centres.
records.text: Water is local: a data centre or fab draws on the same rivers and aquifers as the town next to it, which is where disputes start.

records.title: AI Diffusion Rule
records.description: A January 2025 US rule sorting the world into three tiers for AI chip exports, cancelled before it took effect.
records.text: Issued by the Biden administration in January 2025, the rule would for the first time have limited exports of US AI chips to many countries: close allies such as Japan and South Korea faced no limits, countries such as Mexico and Portugal faced caps, and countries such as China and Russia faced the tightest controls. On May 13, 2025, days before it was due to take effect, the Trump administration rescinded it. The Commerce Department instead warned that using Huawei's Ascend AI chips anywhere in the world breaks US export rules.

records.title: America's AI Action Plan
records.description: The White House plan of July 23, 2025 for AI, with a companion order to speed permits for big data centres.
records.text: The plan, titled "Winning the AI Race," lists more than 90 federal actions under three pillars: speeding up innovation, building American AI infrastructure, and leading in international diplomacy and security. A companion executive order signed the same day, Executive Order 14318, offers loans, grants and tax incentives and faster environmental reviews for data centres needing more than 100 megawatts of new power or at least US$500 million in investment, and opens federal and military land to them. It also calls for training more electricians and HVAC technicians.

records.title: California SB 53
records.description: California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, signed September 29, 2025.
records.text: Written by State Senator Scott Wiener and signed by Governor Gavin Newsom, the law requires large developers of frontier AI models to publish how they apply safety standards and best practices. It creates a way to report critical safety incidents to the state's Office of Emergency Services, protects whistleblowers, and lets the Attorney General seek civil penalties. It also sets up CalCompute, a plan for a public computing cluster.

records.title: China's gallium and germanium export controls
records.description: Chinese licence rules from August 1, 2023, then a ban on sales to the US, for metals used in chips.
records.text: China announced on July 3, 2023 that from August 1, 2023 exporters of gallium and germanium would need licences naming the buyer, end user and use; it cited national security. In December 2024 it banned approving exports of gallium, germanium and antimony to the United States. On November 9, 2025, after a Trump-Xi meeting, China suspended that ban until November 27, 2026, while keeping the licence system.

records.title: China's rare earth export controls
records.description: Chinese licence rules on rare earths from April 2025, expanded in October 2025 to target chipmakers, then partly paused.
records.text: On April 4, 2025 China required licences to export seven heavy rare earths and magnets, in response to US tariffs. On October 9, 2025 it added five more elements, required a licence for foreign products containing 0.1 percent or more Chinese rare earths by value, and said applications linked to advanced chips (14 nm logic and below, 256-layer memory and above) would be reviewed case by case. China suspended the October measures in November 2025 and, on November 9, 2026, extended that pause to January 10, 2027; the April 2025 licences were never paused.

records.title: CHIPS Act award and US stake in Intel
records.description: A US$7.86 billion CHIPS grant to Intel in 2024, much of it turned into a government stake of nearly 10 percent in 2025.
records.text: In late November 2024 the Commerce Department finalised up to US$7.86 billion for Intel, less than the US$8.5 billion first announced. Intel had received about US$2.2 billion of it when, on August 22, 2025, the government agreed to buy US$8.9 billion of Intel stock, nearly 10 percent of the company, paid for mostly with nearly US$6 billion of grants not yet handed over. Intel says the stake is passive, with no board seats.

records.title: CHIPS Act award to TSMC Arizona
records.description: A US$6.6 billion CHIPS Act grant to TSMC for its chip factories in Arizona, finalised in November 2024.
records.text: The US Commerce Department finalised up to US$6.6 billion in direct funding for TSMC Arizona in mid-November 2024, the same amount as its April 2024 preliminary deal. The money is paid out as the company completes project milestones. It is part of the US effort to make leading-edge chips at home rather than relying only on factories in Taiwan.

records.title: Digital Omnibus delay to the EU AI Act
records.description: A 2026 EU law that pushed back the AI Act's rules for high-risk AI systems to December 2027 and August 2028.
records.text: The European Commission proposed the Digital Omnibus on AI in November 2025. The European Parliament approved it on June 16, 2026, the Council adopted it on June 29, 2026, and it entered into force on July 27, 2026 as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Rules for standalone high-risk AI systems move from August 2, 2026 to December 2, 2027, and rules for AI built into regulated products move to August 2, 2028. It also adds a ban, from December 2, 2026, on AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate images or child sexual abuse material.

records.title: Dutch controls on chipmaking machines
records.description: Netherlands licence rules, from September 1, 2023, for exporting ASML's most advanced lithography machines.
records.text: On June 30, 2023 the Dutch government announced that from September 1, 2023, companies would need a licence to export advanced chipmaking equipment, including ASML's top DUV immersion lithography machines (the NXT:2000i and later models). It cited national security and did not name China; the move followed US pressure on allies. On September 6, 2024 the rules were widened to the older NXT:1970i and 1980i models, from September 7, 2024.

records.title: Executive order against state AI laws
records.description: Executive Order 14365 of December 11, 2025, which set up a federal task force to challenge state AI laws.
records.text: The order told the US Attorney General to create an AI Litigation Task Force within 30 days to challenge state AI laws that conflict with federal policy. States with laws the administration calls onerous could lose some federal broadband funds, and White House advisers were told to draft a national AI law that would override conflicting state laws, except on child safety. The order names a Colorado law on algorithmic discrimination as an example.

records.title: Export controls
records.description: Rules that forbid selling certain chips and chip-making machines to certain countries.
records.text: The US rules of October 2022, tightened since, limit China's access to advanced AI chips and the tools to make them. Allies, including the Netherlands and Japan, added their own.

records.title: Georgia's data-centre tax break veto
records.description: On May 7, 2024 Georgia's governor vetoed a bill to pause the state's sales-tax break for data centres.
records.text: House Bill 1192 would have paused Georgia's sales-tax exemption for building and equipping data centres for two years and set up a study of their effect on the power grid. Governor Brian Kemp vetoed it, saying companies had already made plans relying on the exemption. A 2022 University of Georgia review projected the state would give up US$307 million more in tax from 2024 to 2030 than data centres bring in, while Georgia Power said it needed new, mostly gas-fired, power plants to serve them.

records.title: Ireland's data-centre grid connection rules
records.description: Rules from Ireland's energy regulator, December 12, 2025, requiring new data centres to bring their own power.
records.text: Data centres used about 22 percent of Ireland's electricity in 2024, up from about 5 percent in 2015, and are projected to reach 31 percent by 2034. Under the Commission for Regulation of Utilities' decision, new data centres must provide generation or storage on site or nearby that matches the power they draw, and must eventually meet at least 80 percent of their yearly demand with new renewable electricity generated in Ireland. Grid operators had to publish a connection process by March 31, 2026.

records.title: Japan's controls on chipmaking equipment
records.description: Japanese licence rules for exporting 23 kinds of advanced chipmaking equipment, in force from July 23, 2023.
records.text: Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry issued the rules on May 23, 2023, and they took effect on July 23, 2023. They cover cleaning, deposition, heat treatment, lithography, etching and inspection equipment above set performance levels, and apply regardless of destination. Japan is home to major tool makers, so its rules, along with the Dutch ones, extended US limits on China's chipmaking.

records.title: Loudoun County data-centre rules
records.description: The Virginia county at the heart of Data Center Alley ended automatic approval of data centres in 2025 and paused new votes in 2026.
records.text: On March 18, 2025 Loudoun County's Board of Supervisors ended by-right data-centre development, so every new data centre needs public hearings and a board vote. On November 17, 2026 the board paused votes on data-centre and electrical-substation applications for up to 12 months, backdated to September 15, 2026, affecting about 33 applications.
